**An intercept represents the baseline, while slopes represent sensitivity to features.** If every target is shifted upward by 100, an unpenalized intercept can shift upward by 100 without changing the fitted slopes. Penalizing it makes that arbitrary choice of target origin affect the amount of shrinkage. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html)

For an intercept-only model, minimize $\sum_i(y_i-b)^2$. Differentiation gives b equal to the sample mean. Adding $\lambda b^2$ yields $b=\sum_i y_i/(N+\lambda)$, pulling the baseline toward zero. If the targets are temperatures expressed in different units, zero may have no privileged statistical meaning.

This is why many regression implementations leave the intercept unpenalized and regularize feature coefficients after appropriate centering or scaling. It also helps separate baseline prevalence from the effects of predictors in logistic models.

**“Never” is too strong.** A Bayesian or hierarchical model may deliberately put a prior on the intercept, especially when observations are sparse. That can be useful if the prior's center and strength have a defensible interpretation. Check the library convention: some estimators represent the intercept through a synthetic feature that is penalized. The rule is to make baseline shrinkage intentional rather than accidental.

**Technical details and references.**

Intercepts are usually unpenalized because they set the baseline level rather than feature sensitivity. Penalizing them makes the fit depend on arbitrary target centering or feature-origin conventions and shrinks the baseline toward zero. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html)

For an intercept-only squared-loss model, an unpenalized intercept equals the sample mean; adding $\lambda b^2$ yields $b=\sum_i y_i/(N+\lambda)$ under the unnormalized loss. That may be inappropriate when zero has no special meaning.

“Never” is too strong: a prior on the intercept can be intentional, especially with sparse data or hierarchical models. State that prior and scaling explicitly. Library defaults vary, and some implementations regularize an intercept through a synthetic feature, so inspect the estimator rather than assuming the convention.
